The paper presents a new, open-source numerical tool to compute Brownian coating and substrate thermal noise for mirrors with single-layer, thin, reflective coatings.
The tool uses finite-element methods, adaptive mesh refinement, and parallel processing to resolve the thin coating and handle both amorphous and anisotropic crystalline materials.

For the specific case considered, treating the crystalline AlGaAs coating as a cubic crystal increases the Brownian thermal noise by about 3% compared to modeling it as an effective isotropic material.
The numerical results for amorphous coatings agree with approximate analytical solutions, capturing expected effects from edge and coating thickness.
The authors estimate the numerical uncertainty in the coating energy calculation to be approximately 0.1%.
Running the calculations on hundreds of compute cores enabled higher resolutions by increasing the total available memory.
The tool is designed to be flexible enough to incorporate both amorphous and crystalline materials, helping to understand and reduce Brownian coating noise in future gravitational wave detectors.
Thermal noise is also a limiting factor in other applications like atomic clocks, so the numerical methods developed here could be useful beyond gravitational wave detection.
The authors note that the method can be extended in the future to handle multi-layer coatings and incorporate experimental measurements of independent loss angles for crystalline materials.
The paper's primary motivation is to improve the sensitivity of second-generation gravitational wave detectors like Advanced LIGO and third-generation detectors.
Brownian coating thermal noise is one of the most important noise sources limiting the sensitivity of Advanced LIGO in its most sensitive frequency band around 100 Hz.
The authors use the same mirror dimensions, coating thickness, laser beam width, temperature, and elastic properties as a previous experimental study by Cole et al. to facilitate comparison.
The numerical tool solves the auxiliary elastic problem using a quasistatic approximation, where the oscillating applied force is replaced with a static force.
The fluctuation-dissipation theorem relates the dissipated power in the auxiliary elastic problem to the spectral density of the mirror's thermal fluctuations.
Existing thermal noise models typically treat the elastic properties of materials isotropically, which is appropriate for amorphous materials but not for crystalline materials.
